title: TA9-01239
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, is a citizen of Mexico and claims refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
The claimant fears persecution at the hands of the Aztecas drug cartel.

The claimant alleges that, while employed XXXXX in the city of XXXXX XXXXX, he was approached by members of the Aztecas cartel who wanted to sell drugs XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant refused to cooperate with the cartel. In XXXXX of 2008 he made an anonymous phone call to the authorities to report the drug activity outside of the XXXXX where he was employed. In XXXXX of 2008 he came to Canada as a tourist to visit his sister, a permanent resident of Canada. While in Canada, he was notified that the Mexican military had made a number of arrests in the place where he had reported the drug activity. The claimant also alleges that he was told by friends in Mexico that some of the drug dealers were asking about him because they knew that he had notified the authorities. The claimant filed a claim for refugee protection on XXXXX XXXXX, 2008.
The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
The claimant's identity is established through his oral testimony and the supporting documentation1 filed. State Protection

The determinative issue in this claim is state protection. In arriving at its decision, the panel considered the issue of whether the claimant's fear is objectively reasonable. In order to do so, the panel considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in Mexico, whether or not the claimant took all reasonable steps to avail himself of that protection, and whether he has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.

The claimant testified that he was employed as the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in the town of XXXXX XXXXX in the state of Chiguaga. Drugs were being sold outside of his establishment and he stated that, on a number of occasions, he was approached by individuals who wanted to sell drugs inside XXXXX. The claimant stated that he reported these requests to his boss who became fearful. He also stated that, in 2006, he spoke with a section captain of the police about the sale of drugs in the area of XXXXX and the captain told the claimant to keep his mouth shut.

The claimant then testified that, on two occasions, between 2006 and 2008 he had a gun pointed to his head by individuals who wanted to sell drugs in XXXXX. The claimant was asked if he had reported these incidents to the police and he stated that he had not done so because everyone in Mexico knows that the police receive money from drug dealers. He was asked why he had not mentioned these incidents in his PIF and the claimant stated that these things happen all the time in Mexico. I reject this explanation. I find that the claimant did not provide a reasonable explanation for his failure to mention these incidents in his PIF and this failure undermines his credibility.

In XXXXX 2008, the claimant saw a telephone number advertised for people to call anonymously to report drug dealers. The claimant telephoned that particular number and reported the drug dealers who were selling drugs outside of his place of employment. He mentioned to a police friend of his, XXXXX that he had made this call and his friend told the claimant that he should disappear for a while. A month later, in XXXXX of 2008, the claimant came to Canada to visit his sister, a permanent resident of Canada.

While in Canada visiting his sister, the claimant learned from XXXXX, a friend of his in Mexico, that the Mexican military had gone to the area that he had reported in his anonymous phone call and rounded up the drug dealers with the exception of XXXXX XXXXX. XXXXX also told the claimant the XXXXX was looking for him because he knew that it had been the claimant who had made the anonymous phone call. The claimant was asked if XXXXX had spoken directly with XXXXX and the claimant stated that XXXXX had told the claimant that it was common knowledge that XXXXX was looking for him. The claimant testified that he concluded from this conversation that his friend XXXXX must have snitched on him to the drug dealers. XXXXX was killed by drug dealers in XXXXX of 2008.

The claimant was asked why he could not return to Mexico and he stated that, because he had made the anonymous phone call, XXXXX and other members of his drug cartel were looking for him. The question for the board to decide is whether state protection would be available to the claimant were he to return to Mexico.

The claimant stated throughout his testimony that, because of the high level of corruption, the authorities in Mexico could not give him protection. Specifically he indicated that agencies such as the Federal Agency of Investigation (AFI) and the Deputy Attorney General's Office of Special Investigations were the most corrupt of all agencies.

In her oral submissions, counsel argued that the claimant's documentation2 and the Board's own documentation3 corroborate the claimant's testimony as to the high level of corruption within the Mexican police force. However, the claimant himself, during his oral testimony, did provide evidence of the effectiveness of the Mexican security forces. He did testify that, based on his anonymous phone call, the army arrested a number of drug dealers who were working outside of his place of employment. Furthermore, the claimant stated that business owners who allowed the selling of drugs within their business premises were routinely rounded up by the police along with the drug dealers.

I have had an opportunity to read the documentation filed and the submissions by counsel and I find, on a balance of probabilities that the claimant has not established that state protection is unavailable for the claimant in Mexico. There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens. The claimant may rebut this presumption by providing "clear and convincing" proof of lack of state protection in their country of origin. The claimant must approach his or her state for protection, providing state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.4 Evidence that protection being offered is not necessarily perfect5 is not clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens, as no government can guarantee the protection of all its citizens at all times. However, where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protects its citizens, the mere fact it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to justify a claim that the victims are unable to avail themselves of protection.6 The onus is on the claimant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.7

When the state in question is a democratic state, the claimant must do more than simply show that he or she went to see some member of the police force and that his or her efforts were unsuccessful. The burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state. In an established democracy, such as Mexico, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action available.8 Moreover, local failures by the authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.9

The documentary evidence before the Board indicates that Mexico is a democracy with free and fair elections, and that there is a relatively independent and impartial judiciary. Furthermore, although there are ongoing problems with corruption, documentary evidence before the Board indicates Mexico is a functioning democracy.10 I find that Mexico is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country.

The documentary11 evidence indicates that Mexico is not in a state of collapse, and further, has been making and continues to make serious efforts to fight crime and corruption. All 31 states in Mexico maintain a preventive and judicial police force. There are at least 350,000 police personnel spread across 3,000 police forces at various judicial levels, although some estimates are that the federal, state, and municipal police forces included approximately 500,000 agents. The judicial police are the law enforcement branch of the state-level Public Ministry (MP), the Attorney General's Office (PGJ) is responsible for investigating and prosecuting local criminal offences, and the Federal Preventative Police (PFP) maintain order and security. The coordination for Federal Support Forces contains special operations and emergency response and the Regional Security Coordination supervises 34 regional commands. The military is responsible for external security but also has significant domestic security responsibilities, particularly in combating drug trafficking and maintaining order, a role that has been increased significantly over the years due to military training and the perception that it is relatively free of corruption. The country also has a number of other state agencies that address criminality, including drug trafficking, kidnapping and corruption in an effort to assist citizens to obtain state protection.

The Mexican security forces are described as hierarchical, allowing for redress to a higher level if a complainant is dissatisfied with services. There are a number of authorities and agencies which will assist members of the public if they believe they have encountered a corrupt official or if they are not satisfied with the services of the security forces. Mexicans who face police misconduct, inefficiency or corruption can ask the Secretariat of Public Administration (SFP), the Program Against Impunity, or the Office of the Attorney General (PGR) to investigate federal and state police failures or misconduct.12 Also offering redress to Mexicans from corrupt or complicit officials are the National (CNDH) or State Human Rights Commissions and the General Comptroller's Assistance Directorate. The CNDH can receive complaints, but its recommendations are nonbinding and carry no legal weight. However, once a government entity accepts a CNDH recommendation, it is legally bound to take appropriate action. A similar mechanism exists at the state level. Transgressors on the security forces face sanctions, removal suspension or dismissal.13 In addition, the Federal Agency of Investigation (AFI) deals with corrupt state officials, drug traffickers and kidnappers.

Further efforts to ensure police effectiveness and purge corruption include investigations by the Secretary of Public Security, complaints monitoring by the Inspector General, and a 24-hour hotline to report corrupt officials. Security forces have instituted new recruiting procedures, drug testing, economic incentives, education and identification of officers, with sanctions levied against ineffective or corrupt officers including arrests, prosecutions and the convictions of members of the security forces. New government laws attacking corruption and bribery and sentences of five to ten years imprisonment for convicted officials, have reportedly had a marked effect.14

Since the year 2000, the then President of Mexico has made the punishment of corrupt and abusive police officers a priority. There have been significant efforts to eradicate corruption and impunity within Mexican security forces and to foster accountability and respect for human rights.15

There is ample information in the documentation16 to indicate that inefficiency, bribery and corruption remain issues in Mexican security forces at all levels, as well as within the public service sector. I acknowledge and I have considered this information. However, weighed against this is reliable and persuasive evidence which indicates that Mexico candidly acknowledges its past problems and is taking active steps to rectify these matters.

It is accepted that Mexico has had some difficulties in the past with addressing criminality and corruption. The documentary evidence cited previously is drawn from a variety of reliable and independent sources, none of which have any vested interest in the outcome of this claim. To that extent it is relatively free of bias. While there are some inconsistencies among sources, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggest that, although not perfect, there is adequate and adequate state protection in Mexico, that Mexico is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of criminality and police are both willing and able to protect such victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted, are not generalized and they are being addressed. The claimant has not established that were he to return to Mexico today, protection would not be reasonably forthcoming or that it is objectively unreasonable for him to seek that protection.

I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and, as the issue of state protection is equally applicable to claims based on section 96 and 97, his claim must fail.
I therefore determine that the claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim.
